===== FILE 19622__1.pdf =====
1
Public Comment on Docket VA-2025-VHA-0073 
Date: September 1, 2025 
 
 
 
I am grateful for the opportunity to comment on the Department of Veterans Affairs’ 
proposed rule which seeks to ban abortion care and counseling from its medical benefits packages. 
I am a human rights lawyer, and I write in my individual capacity to express my fervent opposition 
to such a rule as it is in violation of the country’s international human rights obligations and has a 
disparate impact on marginalized communities.  
Despite the United States’ historically arms-length relationship with international law,1 it 
is a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (“ICCPR”),2 which 
mandates that access to abortion care is a necessary component of treaty compliance. The United 
Nations Human Rights Committee, which oversees implementation of the ICCPR,3 issues 
guidance on compliance with treaty obligations in the form of general comments.4 General 
Comment 36, issued in 2019, covers the article 6 right to life.5 The Human Rights Committee 
explicitly recognizes the right to life of the pregnant person, not the fetus.6 It has stated in no 
uncertain terms that “States parties must provide safe, legal and effective access to abortion where 
the life and health of the pregnant woman or girl is at risk, or where carrying a pregnancy to term 
would cause the pregnant woman or girl substantial pain or suffering.”7 While this commenter 
does not seek to establish a hierarchy of reasons an individual may seek abortion care, the Human 
Rights Committee finds that the “substantial pain or suffering” element minimally applies to cases 
of rape, incest, and fatal fetal anomaly.8 In every other instance, the United States, as a State Party 
to the ICCPR, must not regulate care in a way which causes patients “to resort to unsafe abortions”9 
as unsafe abortions constitute a risk to the life of the pregnant person.10 
 
1 See, e.g., Anya Wahal, On International Treaties, the United States Refuses to Play Ball, COUNCIL ON FOREIGN 
RELATIONS (Jan. 7, 2022), https://www.cfr.org/blog/international-treaties-united-states-refuses-play-ball. 
2 International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Dec. 16, 1966, 999 U.N.T.S. 171 (ratified by the United 
States June 8, 1992). 
3 Introduction to the Committee: Human Rights Committee, UNITED NATIONS, https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-
bodies/ccpr/introduction-committee (last visited Sept. 1, 2025). 
4 Human Rights Committee, Rules of Procedure of the Human Rights Committee, Rules 76-77 U.N. Doc. 
CCPR/C/3/Rev.12 (2021). See also General Comments: Human Rights Committee, UNITED NATIONS, 
https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/ccpr/general-comments (last visited Sept. 1, 2025). 
5 See generally Human Rights Committee, General comment No. 36 on article 6 of the International Covenant on 
Civil and Political Rights, on the right to life, ¶ 8, U.N. Doc. CCPR/C/GC/36 (2019) [hereinafter HRC General 
Comment No. 36]. 
6 Id. ¶ 8.  
7 Id. 
8 Id. 
9 Id. 
10 See id. (“States parties should also effectively protect the lives of women and girls against the mental and physical 
health risks associated with unsafe abortions.”); WORLD HEALTH ORG. [WHO], Abortion (May 17, 2024), 
https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/abortion (“Unsafe abortion is an important preventable cause of 
maternal deaths and morbidities. It can lead to physical and mental health complicated and social and financial 
burdens for women, communities and health systems.”); DOCTORS WITHOUT BORDERS, Unsafe abortion: A 
preventable danger (Mar. 7, 2019), https://www.doctorswithoutborders.org/latest/unsafe-abortion-preventable-
danger (noting that “[u]nsafe abortion remains one of the five leading causes of maternal mortality, despite the fact 
that it is mostly preventable” and that”[o]ver 29,000 women and girls die annually due to unsafe abortion.”). 

 
2
Although the proposed rule does not ban abortion care outright and instead removes it from 
the Department of Veterans Affairs’ benefits package, it acts as a de facto abortion ban. Those 
who are unable to afford care will likely not be able to receive it, meaning that the government has 
put its thumb on the scale, effectively making the decision for the individual instead of giving them 
any real choice. In the Turnaway Study, a pre-Dobbs study, researchers found that financial 
concerns constituted the most prescient barrier to abortion access,11 and that insurers refusing to 
provide coverage for abortion care was an additional hurdle for prospective patients.12 Those who 
are unable to access care through legal avenues may resort to unsafe abortions, which constitutes 
a risk to their right to life in violation of the United States’ obligations under the ICCPR.13 
The disparate impact of abortion bans and de facto bans on marginalized communities is 
well documented. Abortion bans, and de facto bans such as this one, have a disparate impact on 
members of the LGBTQ+ community,14 poor people,15 Black people,16 disabled folks,17 Native 
communities,18 those in rural areas,19 and immigrants,20 among others.21  
In the United States, abortion bans have always been about controlling Black and Brown 
bodies;22 this proposal is no different. The proposed rule ignores decades of research on the 
disparate impact of such anti-choice policies, forcing members of marginalized communities to 
turn to community support and abortion funds to try to secure funding for care, or face continuing 
the pregnancy against their wishes. The proposed rule continues a long history of marginalizing 
Black and Brown bodies, in particular.  
 
11 DIANA GREENE FOSTER, THE TURNAWAY STUDY: THE COSTS OF DENYING WOMEN ACCESS TO ABORTION 51-65 
(2020).

REPRODUCTIVE FUTURE WE DESERVE (2024); HUMAN RIGHTS CRISIS: ABORTION IN THE UNITED STATES AFTER

22 See RENEE BRACEY SHERMAN & REGINA MAHONE, LIBERATING ABORTION (2024). 

 
3
Access to abortion care is a human right.23 In putting forth this proposed rule, the 
Department of Veterans Affairs abrogates its responsibility to care for this country’s veterans. To 
comply with the country’s international human rights obligations, the Department of Veterans 
Affairs must not proceed with the proposed rule. Making this proposed rule a reality will have a 
disparate impact on marginalized communities, force individuals to continue pregnancies against 
their wishes, and violate the country’s international human rights obligations.  
 
Regards, 
 
/s/ Ashlynn Kendzior
